case_study_insert.main_stem: Verdant Golf Lodge (VGL) is a cooperative in the leisure industry, running an 18-hole golf course and lodge and employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2003 by Marcus Verdant, the cooperative uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. VGL plans to invest $540,000 in a new nine-hole course and clubhouse extension, financed by a $180,000 bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $80, and produces 9,000 units a year, where each unit is one round of golf. VGL faces staff shortages in the pro shop and rising complaints about course maintenance.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Course Operations Report — Q3 2025: VGL recorded 7,200 rounds of golf, with 13% of tee times left unfilled. Member complaints about bunker and green condition reached 22, up from 14 last year. Average time between tee times was 11 minutes. A survey of 900 members gave VGL a 4.1/5 rating, and 66% said the course was good value. Greenkeeping fuel and fertiliser use cost 7% more per round than a year earlier. A skills check shows 8 of 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the leisure centre costs $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Verdant Golf Lodge as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Leisure Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, increasing loan costs for borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.51 to $13.20 an hour, raising greenkeeping and pro-shop wages. (3) Fertiliser and energy input costs have risen 10.4% year-on-year, while spending on leisure and golf memberships grew 3.9%.

questions.question_text: VGL is funding its $540,000 nine-hole course and clubhouse extension with a $180,000 bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for VGL of using retained profit instead of the loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit needs no interest payments or fixed repayment dates, so the cooperative preserves cash while it meets $240,000 fixed costs and the higher greenkeeping fuel cost of 7% more per round. Money not paid to the lender can instead fix the bunker and green problems behind 22 member complaints, protecting the 4.1/5 rating from 900 members.

Point 2: Using its own $360,000 avoids pledging assets for a bank loan, so the existing course cannot be at risk if the new nine-hole course attracts fewer than the 7,200 rounds recorded last quarter. It also suits a cooperative with democratic leadership: members keep control of the $540,000 project without lender conditions, and the 66% who say the course is good value support reinvesting surplus locally rather than servicing external debt. VGL's 7,200 rounds last quarter show members already fund the course, so using retained profit keeps the democratic cooperative intact while the new course is built.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to VGL's course expansion financing.

questions.question_text: VGL wants to attract members to its new nine-hole course while 13% of tee times are unfilled. Consider a local newspaper campaign, a members' referral scheme, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VGL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper campaign: A newspaper advert reaches the local catchment cheaply and can promote the new nine-hole course to golfers nearby. However, print has low response and cannot show the course; with $240,000 fixed costs and a $180,000 loan, spending on broad ads is risky when 13% of tee times are already empty and the 4.1/5 rating from 900 members is the stronger selling point.

Members' referral scheme: Rewarding the 66% of 900 members who say the course is good value to bring friends is low-cost and targets exactly the people likely to play 9,000 rounds a year. Rewards reduce the $80 fee received per referred round, though, and the scheme relies on existing members' enthusiasm; it may not reach beyond the current membership enough to fill a new nine-hole course.

Social media influencer marketing: Golf and lifestyle influencers can show the course and clubhouse to a much wider audience, with the 4.1/5 rating and 66% value verdict giving credible content and measurable referrals against the 7,200 rounds baseline. Drawbacks are that results build slowly and depend on choosing credible reviewers, and the 22 complaints about bunkers and greens must be fixed before inviting public attention.

Recommendation: VGL should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by a modest members' referral incentive. It reaches well beyond the local paper's readership at lower cost than a broad campaign and uses the strong member rating to fill the new course. Newspaper advertising is rejected as untargeted and wasteful given 13% empty tee times, and referrals alone are rejected as too dependent on the existing 900-member base. Fixing course maintenance remains essential to convert interest into rounds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to VGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VGL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspapers and referrals alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: VGL has staff shortages in the pro shop and 22 complaints about course maintenance. Explain two benefits for VGL of introducing job enrichment for its workforce of 50.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment gives greenkeeping and pro-shop staff more varied, responsible tasks, such as owning a section of the course or managing member bookings, which increases motivation and job satisfaction under VGL's democratic leadership. For a workforce of 50 already short-staffed in the pro shop, higher satisfaction should reduce absence and help keep the 11-minute tee-time interval running smoothly.

Point 2: Staff given responsibility for their own patch of the course are more likely to spot and fix bunker and green problems early, directly addressing the 22 complaints recorded against 14 last year. Better course condition protects the 4.1/5 rating from 900 members and the 66% who say VGL is good value, supporting the $80 selling price and the $60 contribution needed to fill 9,000 rounds and justify the $540,000 extension. Marcus Verdant can review absence and the 22 complaints after a small trial before extending job enrichment across all 50 staff.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VGL's shortages, complaints, rating and expansion.

questions.question_text: VGL must train 8 of 50 staff who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the leisure centre. Which should VGL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on the course and in the pro shop is tailored to VGL's own maintenance standards and booking system, costs no fees, and keeps the 8 trainees productive during the 7,200-round season. It can tackle the 22 bunker and green complaints immediately and ease the 11-minute tee-time pressure. Its weaknesses are that experienced staff lose time teaching, bad habits may be copied, and there is no certificate for a cooperative promoting quality to 900 members.

Off-the-job training: The leisure centre course at $700 per employee provides structured, certified greenkeeping and customer-service skills. For 8 staff the stated fee is 8 × $700 = $5,600, small against the $540,000 investment. However, it removes 8 of 50 staff from an already short-staffed operation, risking longer than 11 minutes between tee times, and generic content still needs adapting to VGL's course.

Decision: VGL should choose on-the-job training first, with short certified modules later. It is cheaper, specific to the actual course and avoids worsening staff shortages in the pro shop while 8 of 50 staff are still untrained. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the $5,600 fee and lost shifts would aggravate the 22 complaints and the 13% of unfilled tee times, and consistent maintenance is needed as the new nine-hole course opens. A pilot with the pro-shop team would show whether the 11-minute tee interval and the 22 maintenance complaints improve before VGL commits $5,600 to all 8 trainees and the new course increases demand on the workforce of 50.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of VGL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, staffing disruption and course relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VGL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate VGL's unit cost per round of golf.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Unit cost = Fixed cost per unit + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ 9,000 = $26.67, plus $20 = $46.67. Answer: unit cost is $46.67 a round.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $80 − $20 = $60. Answer: contribution per unit is $60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VGL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Unit cost of $46.67 against the $80 fee shows a $33.33 margin a round, a benchmark for the new nine-hole course and for the 13% of tee times currently unfilled.
2. Break-even is $240,000 ÷ $60 = 4,000 rounds, so at 9,000 rounds the margin of safety is 5,000, a cushion that supports the $540,000 clubhouse investment to members.
3. Contribution of $60 allows pricing tests: a $10 twilight discount to $70 leaves $50 contribution, so managers can judge whether filling empty tee times pays despite the 7% higher greenkeeping fuel cost per round.
4. Managers can compare unit cost with the $700 per employee training fee and the 22 maintenance complaints to decide whether training the 8 untrained staff reduces costs, and review the $20 variable cost against 10.4% fertiliser and energy inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Unit cost = $46.67 | (ii) Contribution per unit = $60 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: $46.67 cost versus $80 fee; break-even 4,000 and 5,000 margin of safety; $60 contribution for twilight discount decisions; and unit-cost benchmarking against $700 training and 10.4% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VGL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VGL's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.19 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.81 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $30,000 inventories + $40,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $95,000; 2025 current assets = $26,000 + $52,000 + $38,000 = $116,000. For 2024, $95,000 ÷ $80,000 = 1.19 and ($95,000 − $30,000) ÷ $80,000 = $65,000 ÷ $80,000 = 0.81. For 2025, $116,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.29 and ($116,000 − $26,000) ÷ $90,000 = $90,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The first ratio rose from 1.19 to 1.29 even though current liabilities increased from $80,000 to $90,000, because cash grew from $25,000 to $38,000 and inventories were trimmed. The second measure climbed from 0.81 to 1.00, meaning VGL can now cover its current liabilities with liquid assets alone rather than relying on the $26,000 of stock, helpful while it repays a $180,000 loan and funds a $540,000 course extension. The caveat is trade receivables, up from $40,000 to $52,000, which tie up cash that could otherwise fix the 22 maintenance complaints; if members or visitors pay late, the ratios may slip back.

Conclusion: VGL's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement does not depend on inventories, so short-term solvency is stronger. The remaining weakness is rising receivables, so the cooperative should tighten collection while keeping enough cash for the extension.Collecting member dues more promptly would support the stronger liquid position.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: VGL is considering discounted twilight tee times to fill its 13% unfilled slots. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VGL of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Lower evening prices should attract players to the 13% of unused tee times, increasing rounds toward the 9,000 target without adding much to the $240,000 fixed costs. Extra rounds at a reduced $70 fee still yield $50 contribution, helping fund repairs to the 22 bunker and green complaints and protecting the 4.1/5 rating from 900 members.

Disadvantage: Discounting from $80 to $70 cuts the $60 contribution on every twilight round, including players who would have paid full price, so revenue may fall if the discount is not offset by extra volume. The insert gives no figure for how many of the 13% empty slots would be filled, so the net benefit cannot be quantified and the decision must rely on judgement. VGL should trial twilight slots on weekdays, tracking whether the 13% empty-tee figure falls without reducing the 66% value rating from 900 members before extending the discount across the whole course.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VGL's empty tee times, complaints, rating and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 10.4% rise in fertiliser and energy input costs will affect VGL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If VGL's $180,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $180,000 = $1,350 a year (0.0075 × $180,000). That is small next to $240,000 fixed costs, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it. The higher rate could make future borrowing for the cooperative dearer and may slightly restrain the 3.9% growth in leisure spending.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.20 an hour): VGL's workforce of 50 includes hourly-paid greenkeeping and pro-shop staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 9,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 180 rounds per worker, so the higher wage is sustainable only if that rate holds as the nine-hole course opens; job enrichment and training the 8 untrained staff can help protect it.

Fertiliser and energy input costs (10.4%): These feed the $20 variable cost on each round and are already 7% higher per round than a year earlier. The insert does not decompose the $20, so only a bound is honest: if the full $20 were exposed, 10.4% × $20 = $2.08 a round, and at 9,000 rounds that is about $18,720 a year (9,000 × $2.08). Even a smaller exposed share cuts the $60 contribution on every round, and the effect repeats with each round played.

Conclusion: The 10.4% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 9,000 rounds and directly erodes the $60 contribution that repays the $180,000 loan and funds the $540,000 extension, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,350 a year on the stated loan and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 180 rounds per worker. VGL should review the $80 fee and act on the 7% higher per-round cost rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to VGL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VGL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
